background.definition: MS is the narrowing of the mitral valve opening from thickening and immobility of the valve leaflets, resulting in resistance to the blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle.

list.listitem: Incidence is closely related to rheumatic fever and has decreased in the United States.
The incidence of rheumatic fever is less than 0.02 per 1000 persons per year.
Rheumatic fever remains the most important cause of MS.
Infective endocarditis.
Degenerative (severe annular and leaflet calcification).
Congenital (Lutembacher's syndrome–acquired mitral stenosis with associated atrial septal defect).
Chronic valvulitis as seen in systemic lupus erythematosus.
Valve infiltration as can be seen in carcinoid heart disease.
Endomyocardial fibrosis.
Rheumatoid arthritis.
Congenital (cor triatriatum).
Drugs and physical agents such as ergotamine or radiation.
Post-surgical in a patient with a stenosed biologic mitral valve prosthesis or a stenosed mitral valve repair.
Unclassified.
Inflammatory process results in thickening, calcification, and commissural fusion of the leaflets.
Thickening, fusion, and shortening of the chordae tendineae also occur. The net effect is distorted mitral valve apparatus and narrowing of the valve orifice.
Obstruction results in increase in diastolic transmitral gradient and left atrial pressures, which are transmitted backward into the pulmonary vasculature.
Symptoms of congestion develop once the valve area is reduced to less than 1.5 cm2, and a further increase in severity reduces left ventricular filling and cardiac output.
Avoid injection drug use to prevent infective endocarditis. C
Maintain optimal oral health and hygiene. C
Antibiotic prophylaxis is required for lifetime if a history of rheumatic fever exists. B
Endocarditis prophylaxis is no longer required for MS without a history of rheumatic fever. B

Short diastolic murmur following an S3
Echocardiogram reveals a mass in left atrium
Carey-Coombs murmur occurs, which is a soft early diastolic murmur
Diastolic murmur is increased during inspiration and reduced during expiration

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria.
On average, there is a latent period of 19 years between carditis and development of MS symptoms. Symptoms usually develop in the third or fourth decade.

The patients are asymptomatic in the early phase, but symptoms are precipitated with increase in blood flow across stenotic valve or decrease in diastole duration with increase in heart rate. Most common symptoms are dyspnea, increasing fatigue, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Not infrequently, the initial manifestation in some may be frank pulmonary edema, atrial fibrillation, or thromboembolism. Rarely patients present with hemoptysis from rupture of engorged bronchial veins. Hoarseness or persistent cough may also develop from compression of recurrent laryngeal nerve by enlarged atrium.
Uncontrolled atrial fibrillation may precipitate congestive heart failure in asymptomatic patients.
A minority of patients may complain of chest pain resembling angina, thought to result from pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and rarely concomitant coronary artery disease.
General appearance may reveal malar rash due to systemic vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension.

Jugular venous pulse reveals prominent "a" wave due to elevated right atrial pressures or a prominent "v" wave due to tricuspid regurgitation. The "a" wave may be absent if atrial fibrillation is present.

Auscultation of the heart sounds reveals loud S1 due to increased excursion of leaflets. As the severity of MS increases with increased calcification and fibrosis of leaflets, the amplitude of S1 diminishes. Once pulmonary hypertension develops, P2 intensity is increased and splitting of S2 may narrow.
An opening snap follows S2 and is best heard at the apex when the leaflets are still mobile. It may be absent if there is decreased mobility of leaflets in the later stages.

The low-pitched decrescendo diastolic rumble of MS is best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position and in expiration phase. The duration of murmur increases with the severity of stenosis and becomes holodiastolic. It may be inaudible in severe MS due to decreased flow across the valve. The rumble of MS increases with exercise, amyl nitrate, and lying down, but decreases with squatting and valsalva.

CXR reveals left atrial enlargement, pulmonary artery enlargement, pulmonary congestion, and in few cases calcification of the annulus. Interstitial edema may present as Kerley B lines in more than 70% of patients with a pressure of more than 20 mm Hg. In severe cases Kerley A lines may be seen.

ECG is insensitive. P mitrale (P wave >0.12 seconds in lead II) is a sign of left atrial enlargement severe enough to warrant valvotomy. Right axis deviation occurs with the development of pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy.
2D and Doppler echocardiography is the most sensitive and specific for diagnosis.
Echocardiography is used to classify the severity of MS by measuring mean gradient (severe >10 mm Hg), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (severe >50 mm Hg), and valve area (severe <1.0 cm2).

Exercise stress echocardiography can help to identify mitral stenosis that becomes severe at high heart rates during exercise. Trans-mitral Doppler assesment and changes in pulmonary artery pressure are measures to assess exercised-induced impacts from a stenotic mitral valve.

2D echocardiography is also used to assess the leaflet mobility, thickening, calcification, subvalvular thickening, and appearance of commissures. These features are used to determine mitral valve score or Wilkins score and are important in determining the timing and type of intervention to be performed. Patients with low score (a mobile noncalcified valve with limited thickening) are good candidates for either balloon catheter or surgical commissurotomy/valvotomy with an optimal outcome.

Order cardiac catheterization when noninvasive tests and clinical findings regarding severity of MS are not concordant, or if noninvasive tests are inconclusive. There is no need for catheterization when clinical findings and 2D echo are concordant.
Other diagnostic tests used to assess MS are mentioned in .

A clinical decision rule was developed in a group of over 3000 patients undergoing valve surgery (aortic, mitral, tricuspid, and multivalve surgery) to predict the likelihood that they will need pacing postoperatively.

Key factors are preoperative ECG findings (left or right bundle branch block and PR interval >200 msec), age 70 years or older, prior valve surgery, and whether surgery involved a single valve, multiple valves, and/or the tricuspid valve.
See algorithms for the management of asymptomatic (), mildly symptomatic (), and moderately to severely symptomatic () patients.
Anticoagulation is recommended for patients with MS and atrial fibrillation, a prior embolic event, or a left atrial thrombus. B
Anticoagulation may be considered for patients with asymptomatic severe MS and a left atrial dimension of 55 mm or greater by echocardiography. B
PMBV is the procedure of choice for symptomatic patients with moderate or severe MS and favorable valve morphology. A
Symptomatic patients with moderate-to-severe stenosis and valve not amenable to PMBV or commissurotomy should receive mitral valve replacement. B

Medical therapy is not recommended in asymptomatic patients with normal sinus rhythm. Beta blockers may be of some benefit in patients with exertional dyspnea and in sinus rhythm by decreasing transmittal gradient from their negative chronotropic effect.
Diuretics and salt restriction may be used in patients with pulmonary vascular congestion to relieve orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Atrial fibrillation in MS patients is associated with adverse hemodynamic effects. The risk of embolic stroke is 7% to 15% per year. Ventricular rate can be controlled with digoxin, calcium channel blocker, or beta blocker. If hemodynamically unstable, immediate electrical cardioversion is indicated. Left atrial radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation during mitral surgery is another effective procedure to restore sinus rhythm. Notably, large studies of management strategies of atrial fibrillation in the setting of mitral stenosis are lacking.

Anticoagulation with warfarin (target INR 2.5) is recommended for patients with MS and atrial fibrillation, a prior embolic event (even if in sinus rhythm), or left atrial thrombus. It may be considered for patients with severe MS who are asymptomatic but have a left atrial diameter of 55 mm or greater.

In centers with skilled, experienced operators, PMBV is the procedure of choice for patients who have favorable valve morphology in the absence of significant mitral regurgitation and left atrial thrombus.

PMBV can be performed with high success and low complication rates in patients with noncalcified pliable valves, mild subvalvular fusion, and no calcium in the commissures. It is recommended for symptomatic patients with moderate-to-severe MS, asymptomatic patients with moderate to severe MS and pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 50 mm Hg at rest or greater than 60 mm Hg with exercise, asymptomatic moderate-to-severe MS, and new-onset atrial fibrillation. PMBV may also be considered for symptomatic patients with less favorable valve morphology who are not candidates for surgery.

Open commissurotomy is an alternative in the presence of contraindications to PMBV such as left atrial thrombus, moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation, and valve deformity. Open commissurotomy is preferred by some surgeons to closed commissurotomy since it allows direct inspection of the MV apparatus.
In the presence of significant calcium, fibrosis, and marked deformity, PMBV or commissurotomy is less likely to be successful, and MV replacement is indicated.

A recent large cohort study found higher 15 year mortality among patients with mitral valve disease receiving a biologic prosthesis compared to those receiving a mechanical prosthesis, in particular among those age 40 to 49 years.
No participation in competitive sports for patient with severe MS, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation therapy, and peak pulmonary artery pressure greater than 50 mm Hg during exercise.
Hospitalize patients with severe dyspnea and with new-onset atrial fibrillation requiring rate control, anticoagulation, or cardioversion.
Also hospitalize if MS and hemodynamic instability exist.
Consult cardiologist when patients have moderate MS or worsening of symptoms.
Atrial fibrillation: ventricular rate control, anticoagulation with warfarin (target INR 2.5), and radiofrequency ablation.
Systemic embolization: anticoagulation with warfarin (target INR 2.5).
Heart failure: diuretics, salt restriction, beta blockers, and eventually surgery of mitral valve.
Infective endocarditis : antibiotic therapy.
Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is recommended for all patients with prosthetic valves. B
After mitral valve replacement with any mechanical valve, warfarin is indicated (INR 2.5-3.5). C
After mitral valve replacement with a bioprosthesis and risk factors, warfarin is indicated (INR 2.0-3.0). C
After mitral valve replacement with a bioprosthesis and no risk factors, aspirin is indicated at 75 mg to 100 mg per day. C
Antiplatelet therapy with either low dose aspirin or dipyridimole when added to warfarin reduces the risk of systemic embolism or death in subjects with a valve prosthesis.
For patients who refuse valve surgery, survival is 44% after 5 years, 32% after 10 years, and 19% after 15 years.
Death occurs from heart failure, thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, infective endocarditis, or hemorrhagic complications; even sudden death may occur.
Symptomatic improvement occurs immediately after the valve surgery.
Recurrent symptoms or restenosis have been reported to occur more frequently with closed than with open commissurotomy or PMBV.
In asymptomatic patients, yearly follow-up with history, physical examination, CXR, and ECG is recommended.
Echocardiogram is recommended yearly if the patient has severe MS or there is a change in clinical status.

Order cardiac catheterization when noninvasive tests and clinical findings regarding severity of MS are not concordant, or if noninvasive tests are inconclusive. There is no need for catheterization when clinical findings and 2D echo are concordant.
Patients with severe MS in sinus rhythm or atrial fibrillation or those with peak pulmonary artery pressure greater than 50 mm Hg during exercise should not participate in any competitive sports.
Patients who are in atrial fibrillation and on anticoagulation should not participate in any competitive sports involving bodily contact.

PMBV can be performed safely in patients older than 65 years, but the success rate is less compared with younger population considering the long-standing nature of MS, which results in heavy calcification and fibrosis.
MS is often diagnosed during pregnancy as a previously asymptomatic patient may present with progressive dyspnea, atrial fibrillation, and/or pulmonary edema.
The normal physiologic response of increase in heart rate and blood volume causes an increase in transmitral gradient.
Mild-to-moderate MS can be managed with judicious use of diuretics and beta blockers and guidance of a cardiologist.
PMBV can be successfully performed during 24 to 32 weeks of gestation in severely symptomatic patients with few or no complications.
With regard to maternal and fetal outcomes, there is a lack of evidence to support the best treatment strategy in valvular heart disease.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Tests Used to Assess Mitral Stenosis.

tr.td: Diagnostic test of choice. Confirm the diagnosis of mitral stenosis, assess severity, and reevaluate with changing signs and symptoms
Used to provoke symptoms and assess hemodynamic response when results of resting echocardiography and clinical findings are discrepant
Used for hemodynamic evaluation when noninvasive tests are inconclusive or there is discrepancy between echocardiography and clinical findings
More comprehensive assessment of the mitral valve and the subvalvular apparatus with more accuracy and reproducibility; may become the future gold standard
Data are limited; not recommended currently
